Ranges marked estimate:true without a source are our own rough estimates and need a local supplier quote before use. Suggested brands/models are research picks pending supplier pricing, not endorsements.
meta.certNote: Look for third-party certification: NSF/ANSI 42 (taste/odor, chlorine), 53 (health contaminants incl. lead, PFOA/PFOS), 58 (reverse osmosis), 55 (UV), 44 (softeners), 177 (shower filters, free chlorine only), 61/372 (material safety/lead-free only, not performance). Scale-reduction devices: IAPMO/ANSI Z601 or DVGW W512.

general.label: No strong concern: taste, hardness and peace of mind

solutions.name: Reverse osmosis (RO) at the kitchen sink, with remineralization
treats: PFAS incl. PFOA/PFOS (look for NSF/ANSI 58 PFAS claim)
arsenic (arsenic V; arsenic III needs pre-oxidation)
doesNotTreat: water at showers, laundry or other taps
scale in pipes and the water heater
bacteria by itself (it is not a disinfection device)
solutions.install: Under the sink, with its own faucet and a small storage tank; needs a drain connection. Remineralization stage adds calcium/magnesium back for taste.

cost.annual: $60–$150 (pre/post filters $30–$60 every 6–12 months; membrane $50–$200 every 2–3 years)

solutions.maintenance: Change pre/post filters every 6–12 months and the membrane every 2–3 years; sanitize the tank yearly.
pros: Broadest reduction for drinking and cooking water
Certified options for PFAS, lead, arsenic, nitrate
solutions.bestFit: Any home that wants the most reduction in drinking water: PFAS, lead, nitrate or arsenic concerns, families with babies.
solutions.certifications: NSF/ANSI 58 (RO). Check the listing for each contaminant claim (e.g. PFOA/PFOS, lead, arsenic V, nitrate).
solutions.suggested: Good: iSpring RCC7-BN/RCC7-BLK (NSF/ANSI 58 system-certified incl. lead, fluoride). For PFAS: Waterdrop G3P600 (IAPMO NSF/ANSI 58 + 53 PFOA/PFOS) or Kinetico K5 (WQA NSF/ANSI 58/53 PFOA/PFOS, dealer network). PLACEHOLDER until supplier pricing.

solutions.name: Under-sink carbon block filter (certified)
treats: chlorine/chloramine taste and odor (chloramine needs a catalytic/chloramine claim)
many VOCs and disinfection byproducts (per claim)
solutions.install: Under the sink on the cold line, often with a separate faucet; no drain needed.

cost.annual: $20–$100 in cartridges

solutions.maintenance: Replace the cartridge on schedule (typically 6–12 months or the rated gallons). An exhausted carbon filter stops working without warning.
cons: Performance depends entirely on the specific certification
solutions.bestFit: Public-water homes that want better taste and lead/PFAS reduction at the tap without RO.
solutions.certifications: NSF/ANSI 42 (taste/chlorine) and 53 (lead, PFOA/PFOS, VOCs).
solutions.suggested: Aquasana AQ-5200 Claryum (WQA NSF/ANSI 42, 53, 401). PLACEHOLDER until supplier pricing.

solutions.name: Pitcher or countertop filter
treats: taste and chlorine; some models certified for lead or PFOA/PFOS
solutions.install: None. Good for renters.

cost.annual: $40–$150 in filters

solutions.maintenance: Change filters often (frequently every 1–3 months).
solutions.bestFit: Renters or a stopgap until a permanent system is installed.
solutions.certifications: NSF/ANSI 42/53 (and 401 for some emerging contaminants); check the exact claim.

solutions.name: Whole-house sediment filter
treats: sand, silt, rust particles, cloudiness from particles
solutions.install: Cartridge housing or backwashing tank at the main line; usually the first stage in front of other equipment.

cost.annual: $20–$120 (cartridges $5–$30 every 1–3 months)

solutions.maintenance: Swap cartridges when pressure drops or on a schedule.
pros: Protects UV, carbon and conditioners downstream
cons: Does not improve water chemistry on its own
solutions.bestFit: Every well system as a prefilter; any home with visible particles.
solutions.certifications: NSF/ANSI 42 (particulate class) where claimed.
solutions.suggested: Spin-down plus 20" Big Blue cartridge housing (Pentair/Pentek, iSpring). PLACEHOLDER until supplier pricing.

solutions.name: Whole-house carbon / catalytic carbon
solutions.aka: "Charcoal" filters are activated carbon. Catalytic carbon is a modified carbon that handles chloramine and hydrogen sulfide better.
treats: chlorine and (catalytic) chloramine taste/odor at every tap
PFAS with PFAS-rated media sized for it
doesNotTreat: bacteria (and it can remove the chlorine that protects pipes from regrowth)
solutions.install: Backwashing tank or large cartridge housings at the main line; tanks need a drain and outlet.

cost.annual: $40–$160 (media $150–$400 every 3–5 years, or cartridges $20–$80 every 6–12 months)

solutions.maintenance: Replace media/cartridges on schedule; PFAS use needs more frequent changes based on levels.
cons: Media life depends on water use and chemical levels
solutions.bestFit: Public-water homes bothered by chlorine/chloramine, and households wanting chemical reduction for bathing as well as drinking.
solutions.certifications: Few whole-house carbon tanks carry a system-level NSF/ANSI 42/53 listing; dealer-built tanks rely on certified media (e.g., Calgon carbons comply with AWWA B604; check NSF/ANSI 61 on the media data sheet). For PFAS claims use a system certified to NSF/ANSI 53 for PFOA/PFOS.
solutions.suggested: Better/Best: dealer-built backwashing tank, Clack WS1 valve + Calgon Centaur catalytic carbon (chloramine) or Filtrasorb GAC (chlorine). Good: cartridge system (iSpring WGB32B, Pentair Big Blue). PLACEHOLDER until supplier pricing.
solutions.limits: Size by contact time: chlorine needs roughly 1–2 minutes EBCT at peak flow; chloramine needs catalytic carbon and about 3–4+ minutes (about 2.5 gpm per cu ft of Centaur); PFAS needs ~10 minutes (vendor guidance in EPA research), which a typical 1–1.5 cu ft home tank cannot give (about 2 minutes at 4 gpm).

solutions.name: KDF (copper-zinc) media
treats: inhibits bacterial growth inside the filter
solutions.install: Usually layered with carbon in a whole-house tank or in shower filters.
solutions.maintenance: Backwash (tanks) and replace media per manufacturer.
solutions.bestFit: An add-on layer in a carbon system or shower filter, not a primary recommendation. Sold only as a layer inside a carbon system, not on its own.
solutions.certifications: Look for NSF/ANSI 42 or 177 claims on the finished product.

solutions.name: UV disinfection
treats: bacteria incl. coliform and E. coli
doesNotTreat: the source of contamination (well cap/casing problems still need fixing)
solutions.install: Stainless chamber with a UV lamp on the main line after sediment (and iron/hardness) treatment; needs an outlet. Water must be clear for UV to work.

cost.annual: $50–$150 lamp each year, plus sleeve $30–$80 every 2–3 years

solutions.maintenance: Replace the lamp yearly, clean the quartz sleeve, keep prefilters fresh. Shock-chlorinate the plumbing after install and retest.
solutions.bestFit: Wells with coliform or E. coli history, springs, shallow wells, or wells near septic systems or livestock.
solutions.certifications: NSF/ANSI 55 Class A for disinfection of contaminated water.
solutions.suggested: VIQUA PRO10/20/30 (NSF/ANSI 55 Class A) or Luminor Class A models, after sediment (and iron/hardness treatment if needed). PLACEHOLDER until supplier pricing.

solutions.name: Air-injection oxidizing filter (iron, manganese, sulfur)
treats: manganese (black stains) with correct media and pH
doesNotTreat: PFAS, nitrate, arsenic (unless designed for it)
solutions.install: Backwashing tank with an air pocket at the main line; needs a drain and outlet.
solutions.maintenance: Automatic backwash; periodic service and media replacement.
cons: Sizing depends on lab results (iron, manganese, pH, H2S)
solutions.bestFit: Well homes with orange/black staining or rotten-egg smell confirmed by a lab test.
solutions.certifications: Media/valves NSF/ANSI 61 for material safety; performance is site-specific.
solutions.suggested: Clack WS1 air-injection (AIO) filter, dealer-built. PLACEHOLDER until supplier pricing.

solutions.name: Greensand / manganese-oxide filter
solutions.install: Backwashing tank; traditionally regenerated with potassium permanganate or used with chlorine feed.

cost.annual: $50–$200 (regenerant and service)

solutions.maintenance: Regenerant handling (permanganate is a strong oxidizer) and backwash.
solutions.bestFit: Manganese-heavy wells, or where air injection alone is not enough.
solutions.certifications: Site-specific performance.

solutions.name: Birm filter
treats: low-to-moderate iron (roughly under 3 ppm) when pH is about 6.8 or higher
doesNotTreat: hydrogen sulfide (can be fouled by it)
solutions.install: Backwashing tank; no chemicals.
solutions.maintenance: Backwash; media every 5–10 years.
cons: Narrow operating window (pH, oxygen, no H2S)
solutions.bestFit: Moderate iron with neutral pH and no sulfur smell.
solutions.certifications: Site-specific performance.

solutions.name: Acid neutralizer (calcite / corosex)
treats: blue-green stains and pinhole leaks from corrosion
doesNotTreat: lead already in the water from other sources
solutions.install: Backwashing or upflow tank at the main line, before iron filters/softeners.

cost.annual: $50–$150 calcite top-off (estimate)

solutions.maintenance: Add calcite media as it dissolves (often yearly). Raises hardness slightly.
pros: Common, proven fix for PA wells
solutions.bestFit: Well homes with low pH, blue-green stains, metallic taste or lead/copper detected at the tap.
solutions.certifications: Media NSF/ANSI 61. Penn State lists acid-neutralizing filters and soda-ash injection for corrosive water.
solutions.suggested: Clack WS1 backwashing calcite tank. PLACEHOLDER until supplier pricing.

solutions.name: Whole-house PFAS media (PFAS-rated carbon or anion exchange)
treats: PFAS at every tap (when sized and verified for the measured levels)
solutions.install: One or two large tanks at the main line, often in series with sediment prefiltration.

cost.installed: $500–$4,000+ (activated carbon or RO for PFAS); whole-house PFAS systems are at the top of this range or above
cost.annual: $150–$400+ per media change; interval depends on PFAS levels and water use

solutions.maintenance: Media replacement based on testing; periodic PFAS testing after the system to confirm it is still working.
pros: Reduces bathing and cooking exposure too
cons: Certification standards for whole-house PFAS units are limited
solutions.bestFit: Homes with PFAS well above EPA limits that want treatment at every tap.
solutions.certifications: EPA notes that current filter certifications (as of April 2024) do not yet show removal down to EPA's 4 ppt limits.
solutions.suggested: Certified POE options: Aquasana HealthShield WH-HS (WQA NSF/ANSI 53 PFOA/PFOS + 3 more PFAS, 165,000 gal), A. O. Smith HomeShield AOS-HS-1200 (NSF/ANSI 53 PFAS, installer channel), Pentair FloPlus Protect 20BB (IAPMO NSF/ANSI 53, 40,000 gal at 5 gpm). Dealer-built: twin GAC tanks sized for ~10 min EBCT. PLACEHOLDER until supplier pricing.

solutions.name: Well chlorination (shock and continuous feed)
treats: iron/sulfur oxidation ahead of a filter
doesNotTreat: leaves chlorine taste unless followed by carbon
solutions.install: Shock: one-time disinfection of the well and plumbing. Continuous: chemical feed pump plus contact tank, usually followed by carbon.

cost.annual: $120–$360 (solution $10–$30/month)

solutions.maintenance: Refill solution, check feed rate and residual.
solutions.bestFit: Wells with recurring bacteria or heavy iron/sulfur where UV alone is not enough. Shock chlorination after any well repair.
solutions.certifications: NSF/ANSI 60 chemicals.

solutions.name: Arsenic or nitrate treatment (usually RO at the tap)
treats: arsenic (RO or arsenic-specific adsorptive media; arsenic III must be oxidized first)
solutions.install: Most cost-effective as point-of-use RO at the kitchen sink. Whole-house media or anion exchange when levels are high or the home needs it at every tap.

cost.installed: Arsenic: $1,000–$4,000 (media or RO); nitrate: $300–$5,000 (RO or anion exchange)
cost.annual: $60–$300 depending on system

solutions.maintenance: Regular testing of treated water; media or membrane replacement.
pros: Targets the two most common health chemicals in PA wells after bacteria
cons: Needs lab confirmation of form and level
solutions.bestFit: Wells with arsenic or nitrate results near or above EPA limits; homes with infants (nitrate).
solutions.certifications: NSF/ANSI 58 with arsenic/nitrate claims; NSF/ANSI 53 for arsenic media.

solutions.name: Salt-free conditioner (TAC / NAC)
solutions.aka: Template-assisted (TAC) or nucleation-assisted (NAC) crystallization, including NAC media such as Filtersorb SP3. Often sold as a "salt-free softener", but it does not soften.
solutions.how: Water flows through a bed of polymer beads that act as templates. Dissolved calcium and magnesium form microscopic crystals that stay suspended and wash through instead of sticking as hard scale.
treats: scale buildup in water heaters, pipes and fixtures (scale prevention)
doesNotTreat: the hardness itself (minerals stay in the water)
spotting on glass and fixtures (water still dries with minerals)
soap lather (it will not feel like soft water)
iron, manganese, copper, hydrogen sulfide (they foul the media)
solutions.limits: Typical maker limits (e.g., Watts OneFlow): hardness 30 gpg recommended max; install on cold water, 40–100°F; pH 6.5–8.5; iron under 0.3 mg/L, manganese under 0.05 mg/L, copper under 1.3 mg/L (passivate new copper for 4 weeks); no oil or hydrogen sulfide; free chlorine under 2 mg/L; phosphate under 3 mg/L. Above these, pretreat first.
solutions.install: One tank at the main line, often with a sediment/carbon prefilter. Many models need no power and no drain.

cost.annual: No salt, water or electricity. Media replacement about every 3 years on common models (e.g., Watts OneFlow) plus any prefilter; ASU's vendor quotes put annual O&M at $0–$80 (2012). Media price: get dealer quotes (PLACEHOLDER).

solutions.maintenance: Replace media on the maker's schedule (about every 3 years for OneFlow; Filtersorb SP3 claims 5–7 years); change any prefilter.
pros: No salt to buy or carry
No brine discharge to septic or sewer
Keeps calcium and magnesium in the water
cons: Does not remove hardness or stop spotting
Evidence comes mostly from lab scale tests, not long-term field studies
solutions.bestFit: Moderately hard to hard water (about 3.5–10.5 gpg) with low iron/manganese, where the goal is protecting the water heater and plumbing with no salt, no brine, no power and low upkeep, and the customer accepts some spotting. Also for sodium-restricted households and anyone who simply will not haul salt.
solutions.evidence: Arizona State University / HDR study (2011, WateReuse Research Foundation with the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, California agencies and the cities of Phoenix and Scottsdale; not industry-funded): one TAC product cut scale by more than 88% vs untreated water in 21-day DVGW-style water-heater tests on three Arizona waters at 60 and 80°C. Certification options: DVGW W512 (scale at most 20% of untreated, i.e. 80% reduction) or IAPMO/ANSI Z601 (70%). No study has measured water-heater efficiency or life with TAC. NSF/ANSI 61 covers material safety only.
solutions.certifications: Ask for IAPMO/ANSI Z601 or DVGW W512 test reports. NSF/ANSI 44 does not apply (it is for softeners).
solutions.suggested: Watts OneFlow (TAC, maker limits up to 30 gpg), or dealer-built TAC tank. PLACEHOLDER until supplier pricing.

solutions.name: Electronic / magnetic descaler
treats: may reduce hard scale in some conditions; evidence is weak and inconsistent
solutions.install: Wraps around the pipe; plugs in (electronic) or clamps on (magnetic). No plumbing changes.

cost.annual: Electricity about $5–$15 a year for plug-in units (our estimate, 1–10 W at about $0.19/kWh); magnetic clamp-ons $0. ASU vendor quotes: $4–$31 a year.

solutions.maintenance: None.
cons: Weak, inconsistent evidence: about 50% less scale in the ASU test, 4–28% in Virginia Tech's 2021 tests, and no clear benefit in U.S. Army (2001), Lawrence Livermore (1996) and NACE (1985) tests
No certification commonly held; no way to check it's working except watching for scale
Does not soften or stop spots
solutions.bestFit: Not recommended as a primary fix. If offered at all, sell as a low-cost try-it option with a return window and honest wording: may reduce hard scale in some homes; results vary.
solutions.evidence: ASU 2011: a wrap-around electromagnetic unit cut scale about 50% (softer, brushable scale). Virginia Tech 2021 (WQRF-funded): an electric-field generator cut scale 4% in standard water and 16% in natural well water; a permanent magnet 5% and 28%. U.S. Army CERL 2001: two magnetic and one electronic device showed no clear advantage over a control in hot-water heat exchangers. LLNL 1996: no beneficial effect from a magnetic device. NACE 1985: none of ten non-chemical devices reduced scale significantly. DOE/FEMP 1998 was favorable for commercial boilers and cooling towers but called the evidence 'mainly anecdotal'. PNNL 2013 (for DOE): 'mixed effectiveness when independently evaluated'. UNL Extension: magnetic treatment is 'unproven technology'.
solutions.droppedReason: Obsolete for our lineup: 0–50% scale reduction in controlled tests (WRF/ASU 2011, Battelle, WQRF) and no reliable effect on water-heater scale. TAC costs more upfront but has far stronger evidence; for a low budget, heater flushing plus an anode check or a polyphosphate cartridge in front of an appliance is more honest.

solutions.name: Polyphosphate / sequestering cartridge
treats: light scale at a single appliance or small system
keeps low iron in solution (fewer stains)
solutions.install: Small cartridge on the line to a water heater, ice maker or whole house.

cost.installed: Housing about $30–$50 plus a cartridge (retail); installed $50–$300 (our estimate)
cost.annual: Cartridges about $25–$80 each, every 3–6 months: roughly $50–$300 a year (estimate from retail prices)

solutions.maintenance: Replace cartridges every few months.
cons: Limited capacity; less effective in hot water
Not compatible ahead of TAC media
solutions.bestFit: Low-budget, point-of-use scale protection in front of one appliance (tankless heater inlet, coffee/ice machine, boiler fill) on cold water, or renters. Not a whole-house hardness solution; weaker in hot water.
solutions.certifications: NSF/ANSI 60 for the additive (and NSF/ANSI 42 for the cartridge where claimed).
solutions.evidence: Battelle 1986 (ASHRAE Trans.): softened, softened plus polyphosphate, and hard water plus polyphosphate all reduced scale in water heaters. NACE 1985: phosphorus-based chemicals cut scale almost completely in a heat-exchanger test. Virginia Tech 2021: a phosphate sacrificial-media cartridge cut scale about 54% (standard water) and 80% (natural well water). Effectiveness drops at higher temperatures; check the maker's temperature rating.
solutions.suggested: Siliphos-type cartridge in a standard 10" housing (e.g., iSpring WGB-DS line or Pentair/Pentek). PLACEHOLDER until supplier pricing.

solutions.name: High-efficiency metered softener (salt or potassium)
solutions.install: Resin tank plus brine tank at the main line; needs a drain and outlet. Bypass outdoor spigots. Set to demand-initiated (metered) regeneration with upflow brining where available.

cost.annual: $50–$150 salt (HomeGuide), plus regeneration water and a little electricity (estimate)

solutions.maintenance: Add salt (or potassium chloride) about monthly; clean the brine tank every 5–10 years; resin 10–15+ years (longer with a carbon prefilter on chlorinated water). Check the water heater anode every 1–2 years or fit a powered anode.
pros: Removes hardness: no spots, better lather, soft feel
Strongest evidence for keeping gas and tankless heaters at factory efficiency (Battelle 2009, WQRF-funded)
Handles low iron/manganese that TAC cannot
High-efficiency metered models use 26–60% less salt than timer models (Univ. of Minnesota)
Can run on potassium chloride for no added sodium
cons: Brine (chloride) discharge to septic or sewer
Uses up the water heater anode faster
solutions.bestFit: Very hard water (about 10.5+ gpg / 180+ mg/L), iron or manganese up to a few mg/L, customers who want spot-free glass, rich lather and soft-feeling water, and tankless heaters above the maker hardness limit (Rinnai: 200 mg/L).
solutions.evidence: Removes hardness (certified to NSF/ANSI 44). Battelle 2009 (funded by WQRF, WQA's research arm): gas and tankless heaters on softened water kept their starting efficiency through a 90-day accelerated test (about 1.25–2.25 years of use), while on 26 gpg hard water gas tank efficiency fell from 70.4% to 67.4% and tankless from 80% to 72% (tankless needed deliming at 1.6 years). Electric heaters showed no efficiency change either way. Virginia Tech 2021 (WQRF-funded): about 100% scale reduction. The '15-year' and 'up to 24%/48% efficiency loss' figures are projections, not measurements. Softened water consumed magnesium anodes much faster (Battelle 1987).
solutions.certifications: NSF/ANSI 44 (structural and performance). Look for the NSF/ANSI 44 efficiency rating: demand-initiated regeneration, at least 3,350 grains per lb of salt and no more than 5 gallons per 1,000 grains (PNNL).
solutions.limits: Can take out low iron, but an iron filter is recommended above about 3 mg/L; chlorine above about 1 mg/L shortens resin life (Univ. of Minnesota). Needs a drain and an outlet; size to hardness and household use. Choose demand-initiated (metered) regeneration.
solutions.suggested: Clack WS1 or Fleck 5810/5812 metered valve with upflow/counter-current brining, NSF/ANSI 44 efficiency-rated where possible (dealer lines: Hellenbrand, WaterGroup). PLACEHOLDER until supplier pricing.

solutions.bestFit: Customers on a sodium-restricted diet or who want no sodium added, and who accept 3–5 times the regenerant cost. Often a cheaper route to low-sodium drinking water is a salt softener plus RO at the kitchen sink.

tank corrosion protection (the main thing that ends a tank heater's life), especially with softened water

Most salt- and water-efficient softener design
Best for very hard water and large households

bundles.title: Hard water and scale
bundles.headline: Protect your water heater, pipes and fixtures from scale
bundles.pitch: We match the fix to your water: a salt-free conditioner for moderate hardness and low upkeep, or a high-efficiency softener for very hard water, iron, or truly soft water.
bundles.claimNote: Softening removes hardness and has the strongest evidence for keeping water heaters at factory efficiency (Battelle 2009, industry-funded). TAC reduced scale by more than 88% in a publicly funded ASU test but does not remove hardness, so some spotting remains.
bundles.requires: TAC needs low iron, manganese, copper and sulfide. Softeners handle low iron/manganese; above about 3 mg/L iron, an iron filter goes first.

bundles.title: PFAS and chemicals
bundles.headline: Cut PFAS and chemicals where you drink, and at every tap
bundles.pitch: Reverse osmosis at the kitchen sink is the most thorough way to reduce PFAS in the water you drink and cook with. Whole-house carbon adds chemical and chlorine reduction for showers and laundry.
bundles.claimNote: Choose systems certified to NSF/ANSI 58 (RO) or 53 with a PFOA/PFOS claim. EPA notes current certifications don't yet prove removal down to its 4 ppt limits.

bundles.title: Chlorine taste and byproducts
bundles.headline: Lose the pool smell at every tap
bundles.pitch: Whole-house carbon (catalytic carbon for chloramine) removes chlorine taste and odor from every faucet and shower. Pair it with RO at the sink for drinking water.
bundles.claimNote: Chlorine is added on purpose to keep public water safe in the pipes; filtering it at the home is about taste, odor and byproducts. Check whether your utility uses chlorine or chloramine before choosing media.
bundles.showerRule: Add a shower filter only if there is no whole-house carbon.

bundles.title: Bacteria in well water
bundles.headline: Chemical-free disinfection for your well
bundles.pitch: A UV system with a sediment prefilter disinfects every drop entering the house. We also check the well cap and casing, because fixing the source matters too.
bundles.claimNote: UV needs clear water and an annual lamp change. After installing, the plumbing should be shock-chlorinated and the water retested.

bundles.title: Iron, manganese and rotten-egg smell
bundles.headline: Stop orange and black stains and the rotten-egg smell
bundles.pitch: An air-injection oxidizing filter removes iron, manganese and hydrogen sulfide in one backwashing tank, with no chemicals.
bundles.claimNote: Sizing needs a lab test (iron, manganese, pH, hydrogen sulfide). If the smell is only in hot water, the water heater's anode rod is a likely cause (Penn State).

bundles.title: Acidic / corrosive water
bundles.headline: Protect your pipes from corrosive water
bundles.pitch: An acid neutralizer raises pH so water stops eating at copper pipes, which causes blue-green stains, pinhole leaks and can pull lead and copper into your water.
bundles.claimNote: Penn State lists acid-neutralizing filters or soda-ash injection for corrosive water. Neutralizers add a little hardness.

bundles.title: Lead
bundles.headline: Certified lead reduction where you drink
bundles.pitch: Lead usually comes from service lines, solder and fixtures inside older homes. A certified RO or carbon-block filter at the kitchen tap reduces lead in drinking and cooking water.
bundles.claimNote: Look for NSF/ANSI 53 or 58 with a lead claim. EPA notes lead pipes are more likely in homes built before 1986. On wells with corrosive water, fix the pH too.

bundles.title: Health-based violation on record
bundles.headline: An extra barrier at your kitchen tap
bundles.pitch: Utilities fix violations at the treatment plant, and many are resolved quickly. If you want an extra barrier for the water you drink, a certified RO system at the kitchen sink reduces a broad range of contaminants. We'll look at what the violation involved before recommending anything.
bundles.claimNote: RO is not a disinfection device. For germ-related violations, follow your utility's notices (such as boil-water advisories).

bundles.title: Nitrate, arsenic and dissolved salts
bundles.headline: Reverse osmosis for nitrate and arsenic
bundles.pitch: Point-of-use RO at the kitchen sink is usually the most cost-effective fix for nitrate, arsenic and salty-tasting water. Whole-house media is an option when levels are high.

honestSellLines: "Reduces scale buildup in your water heater and pipes, with no salt, no brine and no electricity." (ASU 2011 TAC result; use the model's own DVGW W512 or IAPMO Z601 certificate if it has one)

"In an independent Arizona State University study funded by water agencies, this type of system cut scale in a water-heater test by more than 88% compared with untreated water." (say 'this type of system': ASU tested one TAC product)
"Keeps calcium and magnesium in your water and adds no sodium." (true by design)
"No wastewater and no brine going into your septic system or the sewer." (true by design)
"Scale is what robs gas and tankless water heaters of efficiency; cutting scale helps protect it." (general link measured by Battelle; don't attach a percentage to TAC)
"Low upkeep: no salt bags; replace the media every few years." (state the model's interval)
Always say: "It doesn't remove hardness, so you may still see some spots on glass and shower doors. It isn't a softener."
avoidClaims: "Softens your water" or "salt-free softener" without saying it leaves the hardness in.
"Extends/doubles your water heater's life" or "adds X years": no study has measured heater life for TAC (or for any treatment).
Quoting Battelle's "15-year", "24%" or "48%" figures for TAC: Battelle tested softened water only, and those numbers are projections.
"Works on any water": TAC needs low iron, manganese, copper and no hydrogen sulfide, about 30 gpg or less, on the cold line.
"Dissolves existing scale" (not measured in the independent tests).
"DOE-endorsed" or citing the 1998 FEMP alert for electronic/magnetic descalers (FEMP called its evidence mainly anecdotal and covered commercial boilers and cooling towers).
"Magnetic/electronic descalers work like softeners or TAC" (0–50% in controlled tests).
Running down softeners as outdated or unhealthy: modern metered softeners are the best fit for very hard water and iron.
saltFreeVsSoftener.paAngle: Pennsylvania on-lot septic design rules already include water-softener flow in septic tank sizing (25 Pa. Code § 73.31), so softeners are allowed with septic systems. We did not find a statewide Pennsylvania ban on softener discharge. A WQRF-funded Virginia Tech study found efficiently run softeners don't hurt septic tank performance, while inefficient ones (excess salt) can impair settling; chloride passes through septic systems to groundwater (Univ. of Minnesota). So 'no brine discharge' is a fair environmental point, but don't claim softeners damage septic systems. Check the local sewer authority or township before claiming any local restriction. Many PA wells have iron or manganese (Penn State), which salt-free media can't tolerate without pretreatment.
saltFreeVsSoftener.framingNote: We sell both. Use these lines when TAC is the right pick for the home, not to talk someone out of a softener that fits better.

waterHeaterLife.answer: Less scale keeps gas and tankless heaters more efficient and keeps tankless heaters from clogging. No study we found measured how many years any treatment adds to a water heater's life; life claims are projections. For tank heaters, corrosion (anode depletion) is what usually ends their life, and softened water speeds that up unless the anode is maintained.
proven: Battelle 2009 (WQRF-funded, 30 heaters, 90-day accelerated test about 1.25–2.25 years of use, 26 gpg well water): gas tank efficiency 70.4% to 67.4% on hard water vs unchanged on softened; tankless 80% to 72%, delimed at 1.6 years; electric no change; scale 528 vs 7 g/yr (gas) and 907 vs 14 g/yr (electric).

Battelle Columbus 1986–87 (ASHRAE Trans.): 60 lb scale (about 20 years equivalent) cut gas efficiency about 5% and made electric elements fail periodically; 130 lb (about 50 years) cut 12 points and cracked a weld; softened water consumed magnesium anodes much faster.
ASU 2011 (publicly funded): TAC more than 88% less scale; electromagnetic and electrolytic about 50% (soft scale).
Virginia Tech 2021 (WQRF + Spring Point): softener about 100%; phosphate and citric media about 50%; magnet 5% and electric-field generator 4% (28% and 16% in well water).
CERL 2001, LLNL 1996, NACE 1985: magnetic/electronic devices showed no significant scale benefit.
extrapolated: 'Maintained factory efficiency over a 15-year lifetime' and 'up to 24%' (30 gpg, 50 gal/day) or 'up to 48%' efficiency loss: equations fitted to about 2 years of accelerated data.
'Element life can be expected to shorten' (Battelle): expected, not measured.
Any heater-life or energy-saving claim for TAC, citric, electronic or magnetic devices: only scale mass in short tests was measured.

byHeater.tankless: Hard water does the most harm here (PNNL: under 2 years in extremely hard water without deliming). Treat the water; softening has the best evidence; TAC within the maker's limits.
byHeater.gasTank: Scale costs a few points of efficiency over years; flush yearly; treatment optional; if softening, maintain the anode.
byHeater.electricTank: No efficiency loss measured; elements can fail; flush yearly, lower-watt-density elements; softening not required for the heater (PNNL).

waterHeaterLife.note: WQRF says it is repeating the Battelle study starting in 2026.

tenYearCost.label: Illustrative 10-year cost of ownership (estimates, undiscounted, today's prices)
tenYearCost.asuComparison: ASU's 2012-dollar 10-year life-cycle averages (vendor quotes, 300 gal/day, 3% discount): TAC $1,326, ion exchange $3,478, magnetic $855, electrically induced precipitation $4,151.
tenYearCost.notes: Not included: water-heater energy savings (projected, not measured for TAC/electronic), yearly flushing (recommended for every option), plumbing changes, local rates. Electronic is cheapest but has the weakest evidence.

strategy.rule: Sell each customer the best option within their price range. Drop products that are obsolete because something better exists at a similar price.
strategy.change: v0.5 led with salt-free (TAC) for every hard-water case and positioned softeners as the thing to sell against. That framing is retired. We now offer both: a high-efficiency metered softener where it is the best fit (very hard water, iron/manganese, spot-free/soft-feel goals, tankless heaters over the maker hardness limit) and TAC where it is (moderate hardness, no-salt/low-upkeep/sodium/brine priorities, clean water).

tac.headline: Protect your water heater and fixtures from scale, with no salt
tac.pitch: A salt-free conditioner reduces scale buildup with no salt to carry, no brine and usually no power or drain. It does not remove hardness, so some spotting remains.
tac.claimNote: TAC reduced scale formation by more than 88% in a university water-heater test (ASU / WateReuse, publicly funded). It does not remove hardness.

softener.headline: Soft water: no scale, no spots, better lather
softener.pitch: At your hardness, a high-efficiency metered softener is the most effective fix: it removes the minerals that scale water heaters and spot glass. Modern metered, upflow models use far less salt than old timer units.
softener.claimNote: Softened water kept gas and tankless heaters at their starting efficiency in an accelerated test (Battelle 2009, industry-funded). Demand-initiated softeners use 26–60% less salt than timer models (Univ. of Minnesota).

twin.headline: Very hard water needs real softening, around the clock
twin.pitch: At this hardness a twin-tank metered softener keeps soft water flowing 24/7 and uses the least salt per gallon. Salt-free conditioners are not rated for water this hard.
twin.claimNote: Twin-tank systems use up to 30% less salt than single tanks (Univ. of Minnesota). TAC makers cap hardness around 30 gpg.

hardnessTiers.note: gpg = grains per gallon; 1 gpg = 17.1 mg/L as CaCO3. PA examples: Penn State well data statewide median 85 mg/L (5.0 gpg) across 8,244 samples, with county medians from 22 mg/L (Clarion) to 235 mg/L (Washington); Montgomery 188 (11 gpg), Bucks 146 (8.5), Delaware 134 (7.8), Chester 82 (4.8), Berks 62 (3.6); individual wells up to 1,824 mg/L (107 gpg). Philadelphia Water 2025: Baxter 6 gpg, Belmont 9, Queen Lane 10 (max 16). PA American Water Phoenixville 2025 report: 151 mg/L (8.8 gpg) in the distribution system, range 120-220 (7.0-12.9 gpg); water leaving its Royersford plant 155 mg/L (9.1 gpg). The Phoenixville Borough 2025 report lists no hardness. Aqua PA: check the utility report (PLACEHOLDER).

ispring.verdict: Keep iSpring for value under-sink RO, but not as the only supplier. Its RCC7 RO family has genuine NSF/ANSI 58 system certification (not just components), support is US-based, and no CPSC recall turned up. But its certified list is short (14 NSF listings, all RO), nothing is certified for PFAS, the whole-house, softener, descaler and UV lines have no performance listings we could find, and the warranty is 1 year (extended plans sold separately). Use certified alternatives for PFAS sales, whole-house carbon tanks, softeners and UV.
certifications: NSF/ANSI 58 (system-level, NSF): RCC7, RCC7AK, RCC7AK-UV made in Taichung, Taiwan: TDS reduction only.

NSF/ANSI 58 (system-level, NSF): RCC7-BLK, RCC7-BN, RCC7AK-BLK/-BN, RCC7AK-UVBLK/-UVBN, RCC7UV made in Nanjing, China: asbestos, barium, cadmium, chromium (III), copper, fluoride, lead, selenium, TDS. Also NSF/ANSI 372 lead-free.
NSF/ANSI 58 (system-level, NSF): RO500 tankless (BN/ORB, AK variants): TDS reduction only.
Replacement cartridges are certified only as components of those systems.
No NSF/ANSI 42, 53, 55, 401 or P473 listings found at NSF; no PFAS certification (its PFAS models cite SGS lab tests, not certification). WQA/IAPMO directories not fully checked this pass.

ispring.warranty: 1-year limited warranty (repair/replace; only for purchases from authorized sellers; registration required), 1-year money-back on many items via its own store, lifetime phone support M–F from Cumming, GA; 3/5/10-year extended warranties sold separately.
ispring.reliability: No Wirecutter or Consumer Reports test found. Owner reports are mixed-to-good: many 5–8 year installs, with recurring complaints about faucet, fitting and tank leaks (typical of push-fit RO).
ispring.recalls: No CPSC recall or class action involving iSpring found (search Nov 2026).
ispring.dealer: Authorized dealer program: no franchise fee, no inventory requirement, co-op advertising, onboarding, exclusive territories; requires licensing, bonding and insurance. Dealer pricing and margins are not published: request from dealer@ispringfilter.com (PLACEHOLDER).

wholeHouseProviders.cartridgeVsTank: Cartridge (20" Big Blue) systems are cheap and simple but hold little carbon (short contact time) and need changes every 6–12 months. Backwashing tanks (Clack/Fleck valve) hold 1–2.5 cu ft, backwash to prevent channeling and fouling, and last 3–5+ years on chlorine. Non-backwashing upflow tanks (SpringWell, Aquasana Rhino, Pelican) sit in between: no drain or power, media replaced every ~5–10 years per maker.
wholeHouseProviders.pfas: GAC is one of EPA's best available technologies for PFAS (with ion exchange and RO), but contact time decides it: EPA-funded research found a typical 1 cu ft, 4 gpm home tank gives about 2 minutes empty-bed contact time versus ~10 minutes vendors recommend for PFAS, and at high PFAS levels even an 8 cu ft two-tank system needed new carbon in weeks. So: sell RO at the sink for PFAS drinking water, and only sell whole-house PFAS with a certified system (or an engineered, tested GAC/IX design with follow-up testing).
wholeHouseProviders.chloramine: Chloramine needs catalytic carbon (e.g., Calgon Centaur) and about 3–4+ minutes contact (roughly 2.5 gpm per cu ft). Standard GAC removes chlorine easily but chloramine poorly.
wholeHouseProviders.margins: No supplier publishes dealer margins. Practical picture: dealer-built Clack/Fleck tanks with bulk media give the most control over price and service revenue; DTC brands (SpringWell, Aquasana, Pelican) sell retail online, which caps installer markup; Kinetico and Culligan are closed franchise networks. Ask distributors for price sheets (PLACEHOLDER).
